title: Disjoint spectral sets and Rosenblum theory
subtitle: G2 lecture 067000 · expanded companion
adaptation: Expanded, source-grounded mathematical companion: independent derivations, worked examples, vector MathTex, reusable diagrams. Spoken source unchanged.

slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 067000 · The problem and its setting
slides.lead: For self-adjoint Sylvester coefficients, an ordered real spectral gap produces an integral of decaying semigroups.
body: Without self-adjointness there is no such spectral order. A complex contour of resolvents provides a different construction that requires only disjoint spectra of bounded operators. The central question is whether the spectra of two bounded operators are disjoint.

For bounded complex operators on Banach spaces, this is enough for the Sylvester operator to have a bounded inverse. The method is associated with Rosenblum, and its engine is a contour integral of resolvents.
slides.takeaway: Resolvent contours solve Sylvester equations without normality assumptions.

slides.title: Recall the resolvent
slides.lead: Let A be a bounded operator.
body: For a complex number z outside its spectrum, the operator z times the identity minus A has a bounded inverse. We call that inverse the resolvent of A at z. The resolvent is a function of z.

It is analytic away from the spectrum, and integrating it around a closed contour can select spectral components of the operator. For a one-by-one matrix consisting of scalar a, the resolvent is just one over z minus a.
slides.takeaway: The resolvent is analytic off the spectrum and detects enclosed spectral parts.

slides.title: The two-resolvent integrand
slides.lead: Let A act on a Banach space Y and B act on another Banach space X.
body: Our right-hand side C maps X to Y. For a complex number z outside both spectra, form the resolvent of A at z, followed by C, followed by the resolvent of B at z. Call this operator K of z.

Notice the order. The right resolvent acts first on a vector in X, C sends that vector into Y, and the left resolvent then acts on Y. Every composition is type-correct even though the two Banach spaces need not be the same.
slides.takeaway: The two-resolvent product is a correctly typed map between Banach spaces.

slides.title: The cancellation identity
slides.lead: The resolvent identity cancels the unwanted middle terms.
body: With R_A(z)=(zI−A)⁻¹ and R_B(z)=(zI−B)⁻¹, use AR_A=zR_A−I and R_BB=zR_B−I. Expanding A(R_ACR_B)−(R_ACR_B)B cancels the two zR_ACR_B terms.
The remaining expression R_AC−CR_B integrates to C around a contour enclosing σ(A) and excluding σ(B). This is the algebraic core of Rosenblum inversion.
slides.takeaway: A cancellation identity turns a product of resolvents into a difference.

slides.title: Integrate around the spectra
slides.lead: Assume first that a single circle contains all of A's spectrum strictly inside and contains no spectral value of B even in its closed disk.
body: Integrate the cancellation identity around that circle and divide by two pi i. The integral of the A resolvent becomes the identity operator, because the circle encloses all of A's spectrum. The integral of the B resolvent becomes zero, because B has no spectrum inside the circle.

Hence the integral of R A C minus C R B equals C. Because bounded composition commutes with the operator-valued contour integral, we obtain A times the proposed solution minus the proposed solution times B equals C. Existence is proved.
slides.takeaway: The contour encloses the A spectrum but excludes the B spectrum.

slides.title: Why uniqueness comes from the same computation
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 067000 · Why uniqueness comes from the same computation
slides.lead: Suppose an arbitrary map X is given and let its Sylvester residual be A X minus X B.
body: Insert that residual into the same two-resolvent integrand. Using the resolvent identities in the opposite direction, one finds that R A times the residual times R B equals R A X minus X R B. Integrate.

The first term gives identity times X, and the second gives X times zero. The result is X itself. Thus the contour construction is a left inverse of the Sylvester map as well as a right inverse. It follows that every C has exactly one solution.
slides.takeaway: The same contour reconstructs any X from its Sylvester residual.

slides.title: Check the scalar case
slides.lead: Let A multiply by a and B multiply by b, with a different from b.
body: Choose a circle containing a and excluding b. The integrand is C divided by the product of z minus a and z minus b. The integrand has a simple pole at a inside the contour. Its residue is C divided by a minus b.

The normalized contour integral therefore gives exactly that value. We have recovered the scalar equation a X minus X b equals C, solved by division by a minus b. The contour formula is the complex-analytic version of that division.
slides.takeaway: The scalar residue equals the expected reciprocal eigenvalue difference.

slides.title: When one circle is not enough
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 067000 · When one circle is not enough
slides.lead: Disjoint spectra do not always fit inside one separating circle.
body: Take σ(A)={−2,2} and σ(B)={0}. Every disk containing both points −2 and 2 also contains their midpoint 0, so no single circle can enclose the whole spectrum of A while excluding B.
Separate loops around −2 and 2 work. The circle-specific Lean theorem has stronger hypotheses; the general bounded-operator argument allows suitable multiple contour components.
slides.takeaway: Disjoint compact spectra may require several contour components.

slides.title: Connection to spectral projections
slides.lead: For a finite self-adjoint matrix, selecting eigenspaces produces orthogonal spectral projections.
body: Riesz projections generalize that selection to operators with possibly complex spectra and nontrivial Jordan structure. A Riesz projection associated with a contour is the normalized integral of the resolvent around that contour. It commutes with the original operator and projects onto the spectral component enclosed by the contour.

Unlike an orthogonal spectral projection, it need not be self-adjoint for a nonnormal operator. This explains why the Rosenblum proof is so flexible. It needs analytic resolvents and projection identities, not orthogonal eigenvectors or Hilbert geometry.
slides.takeaway: Riesz projections need not be orthogonal when the operator is nonnormal.

slides.title: Existence, uniqueness, and a contour caveat
slides.lead: Rosenblum inversion needs disjoint complex spectra and bounded operators.
body: The resolvent cancellation identity proves that a contour separating the spectra gives a solution. Applying the same contour to the residual of an arbitrary X recovers X, establishing uniqueness. For nonnormal operators the contour inverse remains bounded, but its norm depends on resolvent behavior.
A single circle suffices only when one disk can separate the spectra. Multiple loops may be necessary.
slides.takeaway: Existence and uniqueness come from contour algebra, not a sharp distance bound.
